# The Reckon Cycle {#sec-cycle}

The architecture of Part I has so far described systems as they *run*. Commands arrive, events append, projections materialise, queries answer. The system lives in an eternal present.

Building that system is itself a process. A Division is chartered, planned, crafted, released, and then watched and repaired for as long as it lives. The building has phases of its own; long-lived, paused-and-resumed, with histories worth auditing. The plan for the Lending Division has an identity (*Lending, Q3 2026*) and a lifetime (initiate, open, shelve, resume, conclude, archive). It looks, on inspection, like a Dossier.

This is the recursion the chapter takes seriously. The architectural commitments of Part I (Dossiers, the Pizza, screaming names, command pipelines, process managers) apply not only to the *software being built* but also to the *building of the software*. The latter is itself event-sourced, structurally organised, and process-shaped. The Codex names this meta-system the **Reckon Cycle**.

## Building is a process, not a pipeline

The default mental image for software production is a pipeline. Requirements come in at one end, working software comes out the other, the stages in between are progress milestones the work passes through exactly once. Methodologies that share this image (waterfall in its honest form, the V-model, the simpler stage-gate processes) work for problems where the requirements really are stable and the path really is unidirectional. For most software, they do not work.

The reason is feedback. Information flows backwards along the pipeline as often as forwards. A production incident reveals a design assumption that no longer holds. A failing acceptance test reveals a planning gap. The "forward" direction of the pipeline is fictional; the work flows in every direction, all the time, and pretending otherwise produces methodologies that fight the work.

Cyclic methodologies exist; Boehm's spiral, agile-family iterations, lean-startup loops. They are honest about feedback. They are usually not structurally explicit; the loop is described in prose, taught in workshops, internalised by practice. The Reckon Cycle is the Codex's contribution: a cycle that is *structural*. Each turn of the wheel is a Dossier with a stream and a lifecycle. Transitions are events. Reopening concluded work produces a slip in a stream. The cycle is event-sourced, just like the rest of the architecture.

## The wheel, not the pipeline

A Division builds itself through two long-lived processes: **Planning** and **Crafting**. That is the wheel. Planning designs the work; Crafting makes it real; the conclusion of Planning starts Crafting; and when Crafting surfaces something Planning got wrong, the work turns back. Two processes, one chain, turning as many times as the Division demands.

The earlier drafts of this method had eight phases, then ten. Experience collapsed them. Design is not separable from planning; aggregate boundaries and the desk inventory are the same conversation, so they live in one process, Planning. Code generation, testing, and release are not separable either; a slice is scaffolded, tested, and delivered as one continuous motion, so they live in one process, Crafting. What remains outside the wheel is genuinely outside it, and the chapter says so plainly below.

The two processes each carry the full lifecycle protocol. Planning is *initiated* (usually by a process manager, the moment a Division is chartered), *opened* when work begins, *shelved* when a higher-priority Division takes the bandwidth, *resumed* when it returns, and *concluded* when the slate is firm enough to craft from. Crafting follows the same protocol on its own stream. The back-arrow that matters most is the one inside the wheel: Crafting concludes a slice, a test fails late, and the work returns to Planning to re-order or to re-design. That return is not an exception; it is how the wheel turns.

The wheel is a Division's two-process Application Lifecycle: Planning and Crafting, each a long-lived Dossier with the initiate / open / shelve / resume / conclude / archive lifecycle. Planning concludes into Crafting; Crafting turns back to Planning when late discovery invalidates the plan. ## Each process is a Dossier

The recursion is the load-bearing claim. A process is not a "phase" in a Gantt chart. It is a long-lived Dossier: an identity, a stream of events, a state rebuildable from those events, and a lifecycle.

Consider Planning for one Division. The team has decided to build the Lending Division in Q3 2026. *Lending-Q3-2026 Planning* is a Dossier. Its stream begins with a slip:

```erlang
#{
    event_type => <<"planning_initiated_v1">>,
    stream_id  => <<"planning-lending-q3-2026">>,
    data       => #{
        division  => <<"lending">>,
        quarter   => <<"2026-Q3">>,
        initiator => <<"team-lead">>
    }
}
```

Subsequent slips might be `desk_added_v1`, `desk_removed_v1`, `dependency_identified_v1`, `risk_recorded_v1`, `planning_shelved_v1`, `planning_resumed_v1`, `planning_concluded_v1`. The Planning Dossier evolves through its lifecycle; initiated, open, possibly shelved while a higher-priority Division gets attention, resumed when bandwidth returns, and concluded once the planned slate is handed off to Crafting.

Crafting is a Dossier of the same shape. Its slips are the work of making the slices real: `module_generated_v1`, `test_generated_v1`, `test_suite_run_v1`, `release_staged_v1`, `release_delivered_v1`. Both Dossiers belong to the Division they build; a Domain with fifteen Divisions has many Planning and Crafting streams open at once, each at its own point in the lifecycle.

This recursion has practical consequences:

- **Audit.** Why was Lending released with the configuration it had on 2026-08-14? Replay the Crafting Dossier for *lending-q3-2026*. The slip stream tells you what was decided and when.
- **Resumption.** Why is Planning shelved? Look at the most recent `planning_shelved_v1` slip; the data field carries the reason. When the reason resolves, append `planning_resumed_v1`.
- **Transition.** When does Crafting get to start? When Planning's stream contains `planning_concluded_v1`. A Process Manager (see @sec-pipelines) listens for the conclusion and initiates the corresponding Crafting Dossier. The transition is an event, not a meeting.

The point is not that every Planning meeting becomes a stream entry; that direction lies madness. The point is that *decisions and transitions* are streamed; the meeting outputs become slips; the audit trail accumulates without anyone tracking it manually.

## The walking-skeleton doctrine

Before the wheel turns even once at full speed, it must turn once at toy speed.

The doctrine: on day one of any new Division, ship an end-to-end thin slice at minimal scope. One Dossier-initialisation Desk. One projection. One query. Wired to the event store, deployed to all environments, verified working. No features beyond that. Just enough to prove the path is walkable. The walking skeleton lives in Crafting; it is the first thing Crafting delivers, before any business slice.

The checklist:

- [ ] Codebase scaffold (CMD, PRJ, QRY apps; the slicing in place; the Pizza diagrammable)
- [ ] CI/CD pipeline (build, test, deploy stages, all green)
- [ ] GitOps repositories for each environment (test, staging, production)
- [ ] One Desk: typically `initialize_{dossier}_v1`, which creates an empty Dossier on demand
- [ ] One projection writing one read-model table
- [ ] One QRY endpoint that reads from that table
- [ ] Telemetry plumbed from end to end
- [ ] Deployed to all environments
- [ ] Verified working with a probe (issue the command in test, observe the read-model update, query and confirm)

This is Cockburn's walking skeleton, brought into the cyclic framing. The skeleton's value is not the features it provides (none) but the *paths it proves walkable*. Every later feature lands on top of paths that already work. The first deployment is the most informative one; if the release path cannot ship a near-empty Division, it will not ship a full one, and discovering that now costs ten times less than discovering it three months later under real release pressure.

The skeleton is the first lap of the wheel. The wheel keeps turning, faster, with more cargo, after that.

## The two processes, walked

What follows is one section per process, focused on identity and outputs. Detailed practice lives in the team's own runbooks; the Codex's claim is that each process is *real work* with a *Dossier shape*, not an item in a project plan.

### Planning

Planning designs the work. For the Division chartered by Discovery, the team works out the Pizza: the CMD slices needed, the projections and queries the read side requires, the integration facts the Division emits and consumes. Aggregate boundaries are drawn; domain events are named; Decisions are chosen where a Dossier would be ceremony. The slice inventory becomes a sequence, with dependencies noted (this Desk requires that projection; this projection requires that integration fact) and an order, a cadence, and an estimate committed. The Planning Dossier records the design decisions, the alternatives considered, the rationale, and the plan. It may shelve and resume freely as priorities shift. Planning concludes when the slate is *implementable*; not perfect, not unanimous, just firm enough to start Crafting. Output: a design, a slice inventory, an integration contract, and a build plan with appropriate uncertainty bars.

### Crafting

Crafting makes the work real. Each slice listed in Planning becomes a folder in the Pizza, scaffolded first (command, event, handler, supervisor, projection placeholder), then tested, then fully implemented. Testing is not a separate process; unit tests run continuously, and integration, acceptance, performance, and security tests run as the slices land. Release is not a separate process either; the GitOps repositories for each environment receive the new version, the cluster reconciles to it, health checks pass. The Crafting Dossier tracks per-slice progress and the release motion; its slips are typically routine (`module_generated_v1`, `test_suite_run_v1`, `release_delivered_v1`). Crafting's back-arrow is routine too: an acceptance failure or a late performance problem returns to Planning to re-order or re-design. Crafting concludes when the planned slate is delivered to production and meets its acceptance criteria. Output: a running Division.

## Two scopes that are not the wheel

The wheel is a Division's lifecycle. Two kinds of work sit outside it, and conflating them with the wheel is the mistake earlier drafts made. They are drawn as the panels flanking the wheel in @fig-cycle.

**The Domain charter.** Above the wheel sits the Domain. A Domain has its own short lifecycle: it is *set up* once (the endeavour is named, the brand and the strategic intent are fixed) and then it *discovers Divisions* over its whole life. Discovery is long-lived; it identifies bounded contexts, integration boundaries, and the Dossier shapes inside each Division. When Discovery concludes that a Division is worth building, it emits `division_identified_v1`, and a Process Manager initiates that Division's Planning. The Domain charters; it does not craft. Setup and Discovery are Domain processes, not rim stages of any Division's wheel.

**Continuous operations.** Beside the wheel runs everything that happens for as long as a Division is alive: monitoring its telemetry, rescuing it when an incident is declared, debugging, refactoring. These are not phases the Division passes through once and leaves behind; they run continuously, in parallel with the wheel, against the live system. Monitoring is mostly silent; the absence of a slip is the normal state, and the presence of one (`latency_threshold_crossed_v1`, `error_rate_anomalous_v1`) is information. Rescue opens a Dossier when something breaks (`incident_declared_v1`, `mitigation_applied_v1`, `root_cause_identified_v1`, `incident_resolved_v1`, `postmortem_completed_v1`) and feeds the wheel: a postmortem that finds a design flaw turns Crafting back to Planning. Operations are recorded as Dossiers and audited like everything else, but they belong to the running node's continuous life, not to the build lifecycle.

The discipline of the separation is the whole point. A team that treats monitoring as "the phase after deployment" stops monitoring when the phase is over. A team that knows monitoring is continuous never stops.

## Transitions are events

Between Planning and Crafting, and between the Domain and a Division, work flows via events. *Planning concludes*; a `planning_concluded_v1` slip enters the Planning Dossier. A Process Manager (the same pattern as @sec-pipelines) subscribes to that event and dispatches an `initiate_crafting_v1` command into the Crafting Department. The new Crafting Dossier opens, carrying Planning's output as input. One level up, Discovery's `division_identified_v1` triggers `initiate_planning_v1` the same way. The wiring is the Process Manager chain, end to end.

This is the recursion at work. The build process is wired the same way as the systems it builds. The integration between processes uses the same Process Managers, the same Pizza Architecture, the same Dossier shape. Reusing the architecture saves invention (the team already knows how to think about PMs from building production code) and saves substrate (the same event store, the same projections, the same query patterns serve the meta-system).

Implementation note: the meta-system is typically deployed as its own Division (often called something like *guide_venture*) with its own CMD/PRJ/QRY structure. The Divisions it tracks are external; the meta-Division coordinates them via events on the mesh. The recursion is real but not infinite; the meta-Division is itself built with Planning and Crafting, and that is where the recursion stops.

::: {.callout-note}
## Counterclaim and response

**Counterclaim:** *This is just SAFe / Scrum / waterfall with new names. Two processes are still gates; gates are bureaucracy; bureaucracy slows teams down.*

**Response:** SAFe and similar frameworks prescribe *procedure*: who attends which meeting, what artefacts each ceremony produces, how stories flow through which boards. The Reckon Cycle prescribes *structure*: Planning and Crafting are real work with real Dossiers; transitions are events; back-arrows are recorded. The Codex does not say what a Planning meeting should look like; it says that Planning's decisions accumulate as slips in a stream. Teams adapt the ceremony to fit their context; the Dossier shape stays the same. A team that wants to run the cycle with a single weekly meeting can; a team that wants daily standups can; both produce the same Dossiers. The discipline is in the recording, not in the meeting.

The "gates" framing is also wrong on its face. The wheel turns *concurrently*: Planning of one Division runs while Crafting of another and the continuous operations of a third all happen simultaneously. The processes are *kinds of work*, not *positions in a queue*. A team with three Divisions has many active Dossiers across many processes at any given moment; the cycle rolls them all in parallel.
:::

## What this enables

With the Reckon Cycle, the meta-question (*how do we organise the building of this software*) has the same answer as the question Part I has been answering all along: Dossiers in the Pizza, transitions via PMs, integration through events. The architecture is recursive. The discipline scales.

Part II is now possible. With the patterns of Part I in place, Part II walks the actual libraries that make the patterns real: *reckon-db* as the event store, *evoq* as the framework that formalises the patterns as Erlang behaviours, *reckon-gateway* and *reckon-proto* as the polyglot ingress. The library worked example in @sec-library brings everything together. The remainder of the book is, in effect, a guided tour of the working implementations of Part I's commitments.

The patterns precede the libraries. The libraries respect the patterns. Read Part I as the *why*; read Part II as the *how*.
